transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-20T16:00:00-08:00
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (BrightHealth CTO), Sanjay Patel (BrightHealth Lead ML), Lisa Gomez (BrightHealth Security)
---
Summary: quick console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis, request logs, and how to map requests to traces for debugging. Customer wants: clear audit trail, low-latency error root cause, and integration with their observability pipeline.
Topics: tracing UI, request logs export, error analysis flow, sampling policies, RBAC for logs, KMS/retention, demo of a failed request and rollback.
---
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood, i'm the account exec, with priya from our solutions eng team. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Mark Reynolds: good, thanks. excited to see the tracing stuff — we've got a few incidents last month where requests got weird latency spikes.
[00:20] Priya Desai: great, i'll take most of the demo; quick agenda, i'll show the tracing timeline, request-level logs, error analysis, and then a short bit on exporting logs to your splunk and also RBAC controls. sound ok?
[00:33] Sanjay Patel: yep sounds good, we care about being able to tie a token-level cost to specific endpoints and also resolve root causes quickly.
[00:43] Lisa Gomez: also need to understand retention and encryption, like KMS for private deployments.
[00:50] Priya Desai: totally, we'll cover retention and KMS in the security panel at the end. ok, jumping in...
[01:05] Priya Desai: so here's the console, on the left you can see routes and models. i'm going to click into a trace for a sample request. notice the timeline at top — each segment is a hop: gateway, routing, model inference, and postprocessing. you can expand KV cache hits — sometimes spoken as KV "cash" in the logs, which is a hiccup in auto-transcription — but we log it as KV cache.
[01:30] [screen share glitch] Speaker 1: --can everyone see the trace?
[01:34] Mark Reynolds: yep, looks good but the zoom on the timeline is small. can you show the raw request log side-by-side?
[01:40] Priya Desai: yes, toggling split view. on the right is the request log; each entry has request_id, model_version, tokens_in/tokens_out, latency_ms and error_code if any. we also attach route metadata and customer_id.
[02:02] Sanjay Patel: how do we map a request id from our app logs to this console trace? we have a proxy that injects a request header.
[02:10] Priya Desai: you can pass x-redwood-request-id header; the console will group by that and you can search by header, user_id, or request_id. we'll show an example.
[02:25] [typing noises]
[02:40] Priya Desai: here's a failed request example — error_code 502 from model runtime during longer context. timeline shows exec time spiked, and under error analysis we show the stack snippet and the nearest retry attempt. note the automatic fallback — in your policy you can route to a smaller model or dedicated pool.
[03:05] Mark Reynolds: is that fallback automatic or do we opt in?
[03:09] Priya Desai: you configure policies per route; default is no automatic fallback for tenants unless enabled — for enterprise accounts we recommend enabling model-variant fallback with specific SLAs.
[03:22] Lisa Gomez: retention — how long are these request logs kept? we need 12 months for audit but only 90 days hot.
[03:29] Alex Chen: for hosted customers we have tiered retention; you can archive to S3 with server-side encryption and our Private deployment supports your KMS / HSM integrations. we'll send the exact SOC2 and retention docs after the call.
[03:45] Priya Desai: back to demo — you can click any span and see the raw payload and headers (we redact PII by default but you can configure the masking rules). here's an example where input contained a PHI-like token and you can see the masked characters in the payload.
[04:10] Sanjay Patel: how does masking interact with debugging? sometimes we want full payload for reproducing bugs.
[04:16] Priya Desai: for Dedicated or Private deployments you can opt into more permissive logging under strict access control; RBAC + audit logs will record who accessed the unmasked view. for hosted we default to masked.
[04:32] [crosstalk]
[04:35] Mark Reynolds: what about exporting traces — can we push to datadog or splunk?
[04:39] Priya Desai: yes, we have native export connectors for Datadog and Splunk via webhooks or by streaming logs to your S3 bucket; we also have a lightweight agent to forward in near real-time. we showed Splunk in another demo — we'll attach the connector guide.
[04:57] Alex Chen: competitors question — how is this different from anthro.. anthropic or openai telemetry?
[05:05] Priya Desai: good question — vendor telemetry tends to be request-level only; Redwood ties traces to model-level internals (kv cache hits, token batching, kernel selection) and gives you routing/policy metadata. it helps you differentiate latency due to network vs batching vs model exec.
[05:25] Sanjay Patel: can we query traces programmatically?
[05:28] Priya Desai: yes, we have an API endpoint to query traces and to bulk export. sample curl is in the docs.
[05:40] Priya Desai: now demonstrating error analysis view — it surfaces correlated errors, most common stack frames, and a histogram of latency per model version so you can detect regressions after a rollout. here's an example where v2.1 has a 95th percentile jump.
[06:05] Mark Reynolds: that's useful — we had a release that increased tail latency. can we alert on those regressions?
[06:10] Priya Desai: yes, Redwood Optimize ties into this — you can set alerts on per-route percentile thresholds and it will automatically trigger a canary rollback or notify the oncall channel.
[06:22] Lisa Gomez: on compliance, does the console record who exported logs and when? we need audit trails.
[06:28] Priya Desai: audit logs record admin actions, exports, and view events; for Private deployments those logs can be shipped to your SIEM.
[06:40] [minute marker distraction]
[06:44] Mark Reynolds: quick question — sample rates for tracing, we don't want 100% because of cost.
[06:50] Priya Desai: sampling policies are per-route: fixed rate, adaptive (based on error spike), or reserve for 100% for a subset of user_ids. you can also configure token-level sampling to avoid huge contexts.
[07:04] Sanjay Patel: when tracing for low-latency endpoints, any best practices?
[07:09] Priya Desai: yes, enable prefix/KV caching and set lower sampling for p95-sensitive routes; use dedicated capacity for guaranteed tail latency; set smaller batch sizes. we can share a tuning doc.
[07:22] Alex Chen: okay let's do a quick restore/repro flow. priya, show the replay path.
[07:27] Priya Desai: sure — from a trace you can click "replay" which constructs a sanitized request payload and you can replay against a model variant in an isolated test environment. note this is permitted in Dev and Dedicated modes with permission.
[07:45] Mark Reynolds: excellent. for the pilot we want to run throughput tests and capture traces for 3 endpoints. can you include sample curl commands and the request header we need to inject?
[07:55] Priya Desai: yes, we'll add that to the pilot pack.
[08:02] Alex Chen: wrapping up, any other blockers?
[08:05] Mark Reynolds: security signoff timeline — lisa will need SOC2 and arch doc.
[08:09] Lisa Gomez: yes, and an example of RBAC roles.
[08:12] Alex Chen: we'll send SOC2, network arch, and RBAC samples. priya will share the quick benchmark and trace export example.
[08:20] Priya Desai: action items: i'll share the spreadsheet and a sample trace export; alex will send SOC2 and KMS notes.
[08:28] Mark Reynolds: thanks, this was helpful.
[08:31] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with those docs and schedule the pricing/pilot follow-up for next week.
---
Post-call notes: Customer is leaning toward a Dedicated pilot to guarantee tail latency; security is gating on SOC2 and KMS integration. next meeting: pricing + pilot scope (Alex to coordinate).
